prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength bring atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my single preferred part, and the exchange has made me more sure, not less. The physics is one idea: choose the wavelength of the trapping light so that the light shift is the same for both clock states, so that thousands of atoms can be held without Doppler and recoil shifts and interrogated together. Katori proposed it and first showed it work with strontium, and Ye's group carried it to the 10^-18 regime and into many-body clock physics. The result is reproduced and cross-compared in several laboratories, and the agreement is now far below the caesium standard. It is built on atomic structure, where I can judge the quality of the argument myself. The uncertainty budget rests on a few well-understood shifts: the blackbody shift, which is controlled by measuring the polarizability and by cryogenic or carefully characterised environments, and the higher-order and hyperpolarizability light shifts, which are determined experimentally by varying the lattice depth. Independent groups reach consistent numbers, and that is what makes me trust the 10^-18 claim and not merely a single laboratory's statement. The consequences are concrete: centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, limits on drifts of constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, and the road to a new second. Two names, one citation, a result nobody expects to be revised. I do not hold it because the committee leans that way. I held it first in my opening ballot, before I knew who else would.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one my own temperament raises, namely whether this is a discovery of something unexpected or a very fine instrument. I said publicly that I care about that boundary. My answer is that the lattice clock is not merely a better version of an old device: it is a new regime, in which a many-body ensemble is used instead of a single ion, and it already produces physics results in redshift measurements and constraints on new physics. Still, a colleague can fairly say that the discovery content so far is capability and bounds, and I cannot prove otherwise. The second weakness is credit. Takamoto and Lemonde, with the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, are not covered by two names, and the record on who first demonstrated the scheme has not been checked by this committee. The third is overlap with 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion control), which I think is answerable but not nothing. Against B036 I have to say that it is a real new class of matter with a stable interpretation, but its credit chain is genuinely contested, and I cannot judge that from my own field.

responses.point: Pearce asked, as an outsider to atomic physics, whether the blackbody and lattice light-shift evaluation is robust enough to support the 10^-18 claim, and he moved to B025 while deferring to atomic colleagues on priority.
responses.response: You asked me directly, so here is my answer as a theorist who has worked on these shifts. Blackbody radiation is the largest correction for strontium and ytterbium at room temperature, of order 10^-15 in fractional frequency, so a 10^-18 clock needs it known to a tenth of a percent. That is achieved by measuring the dc polarizability and the temperature of the environment, or by operating in a cryogenic enclosure, and it is checked between independent laboratories. The lattice light shift is handled by operating near the magic wavelength and by extrapolating to zero depth, with the hyperpolarizability term measured and found small. I regard the 10^-18 level as supported, with the honest caveat that the claim is limited by the weakest systematic in each laboratory and that the nearby theory, such as the dynamic polarizability and its magic-wavelength dependence, should be summarised in an expert report so we do not decide on my assertion alone. I would ask the experts to check these points specifically, because that is the one place where a quantitative error could undermine the citation.

responses.point: Kroll treats Takamoto's strontium demonstration as part of Katori's own group's credit, and discloses that he spent a PhD year in John Hall's laboratory, where Ye was later trained, leaving recusal to the Chair.
responses.response: I agree that Takamoto belongs with Katori for the first demonstration, since it came from Katori's laboratory, and I would let the citation rest on the proposal and first realisation of the scheme together with the accuracy reached later, so that no priority ruling on others is needed. I would not make Lemonde and the SYRTE work disappear, but their role was in clock comparison and in the early lattice work and does not change the two names, as far as I can judge. On your disclosure, my view is that it needs disclosure and no recusal. You describe a mentor-lineage link in one generation of a laboratory, not a collaboration, a funding tie or a joint paper with either laureate, and a committee that excluded everyone with such a link would have nobody left to discuss atomic physics. I would ask the Chair to record it and to confirm that nobody objects.

responses.point: Mehlig sees B025 as a strong precision-measurement achievement but is not sure it is a discovery, and he would not resist it if it proved more mature and better attributed than B036.
responses.response: That is exactly the test, and I think B025 passes it on attribution: two names that every member who ranked it proposed independently, with no one contesting them. On the discovery question I will not claim more than I can defend. What the lattice clock delivered is a measurement regime that makes new tests of nature possible, and a few of these are already made. If you ask me which of the two I could defend to a sceptical physicist, I can describe the lattice clock in a few sentences with a picture, and that matters to me. On B036 I accept your point that the 2016 prize left the time-reversal-invariant class open, and I have moved from regarding the overlap as serious to regarding it as manageable. What keeps me from moving is not overlap but credit: Bernevig and Hughes are alive, and three names cannot honestly cover the chain.

responses.point: Danielsson holds the Higgs discovery (B003) first with reduced confidence, and he answered my reservation about crediting a few individuals by saying the experiments were led by identifiable people.
responses.response: I accept your correction on one point: ranking it eighth was a statement about attribution and about my own inability to judge the particle-physics side, and not a claim that the Higgs is a minor result. It is not. The discovery completed the Standard Model, and I defer to you on it. Where we differ is in what the committee can do under the three-name rule. I cannot see from the file that the spokespersons were decisive for the detection, as opposed to the leaders of an effort of thousands, and you yourself say you would move if the reports cannot support the names. Given that, I think the committee is better placed to reward a result where the names are not in doubt this year. I would ask you whether you would regard B025 as an acceptable fallback, and not only B036.

responses.point: Olsson prefers aberration correction (B008), values a tool that changed what a community can observe, and says she would not block B025 and might move to it if the priority of the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration is confirmed.
responses.response: I accept your distinction between a tool that changes a community and one that changes a measurement, and I also accept that a direct image needs no theory to be read. But I would not describe the clock as a single measurement: it is now a platform used in many laboratories for frequency comparison, redshift and constants tests. On your priority condition I can give you what I know. The magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstration both came from Katori's laboratory, in 2003 and shortly afterwards, before the high-accuracy work of other groups. Your condition does not seem to me to change the two names, but I would ask the experts to confirm it in writing. On B008 I would add that the TEM and STEM corrector question you raised yourself is the same kind of problem as the Takamoto and Lemonde one, but with a visible competing laboratory, and that favours the clock on credit.

uncertainties: Whether the experts confirm the priority record, that the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock demonstration are Katori's, and that the Takamoto and Lemonde work does not require changing the two names.
Whether the committee accepts that a measurement regime opening tests of constants, redshift and dark matter is a physics achievement and not only metrology, next to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the blackbody and lattice light-shift evaluations, which I believe are robust, are confirmed in an independent expert summary at the quoted 10^-18 level.
Whether the Th-229 nuclear clock stays outside the citation, which I strongly prefer.
Whether the credit chain for B036 can be settled well enough to make it a better choice than B025, a question I cannot answer from my own field.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with Lund and ETH attosecond groups. None of the credited names for B025 (Katori, Ye) appears among my listed collaborators, and I know of no personal or institutional tie to either. I work in atomic structure theory, which is adjacent to the clock field, and I flag that closeness of field and the fact that I have worked on the kind of level-shift calculations discussed above. I have no connection to the credited names on B036 or B022. In response to Kroll's disclosure, I regard a mentor-lineage link as a matter of disclosure and not recusal, and I leave the final judgement to the Chair.
